name: First Kashmir War
summary: War between India and Pakistan over the princely state of Jammu and Kashmir after the Maharaja’s accession, ending in a UN-supervised ceasefire and the Line of Control.
scaleRationale: Interstate war that froze a still-disputed boundary.

name: Hyderabad, 1948
summary: Indian military operation that ended the Nizam’s holdout princely state. Followed by contested mass violence against Muslims in the countryside.
scaleRationale: State integration plus a killing wave whose scale is still argued.

sources.title: Sunderlal Committee report (long suppressed)
sources.creator: Government of India
sources.note: Often cited around 30–40,000; figures remain disputed.

killed.note: Military deaths were small; civilian killings after the operation are the disputed mass.

historiography.claim: A police action with limited fighting.
A communal massacre in the wake of the army’s arrival.

name: Goa, 1961
summary: Indian operation that ended Portuguese rule in Goa, Daman and Diu after fourteen years of diplomacy and blockade.
scaleRationale: Short interstate operation, limited battle deaths, large political consequence.

sources.title: Indian Ministry of Defence official history, 1961 operations

name: Sino-Indian War, 1962
summary: Month-long war on the Himalayan border, mainly in NEFA (Arunachal) and Ladakh / Aksai Chin. Ceasefire left the territorial dispute intact.
scaleRationale: Interstate war; the Northeast was a battlefield, not a side story.

name: Naga insurgency
summary: The longest running insurgency in India. Naga nationalist claims predate the Republic; armed conflict with the Indian state stretches from the 1950s through ceasefires, splits, and talks that are still open.
scaleRationale: Decades, multiple states, AFSPA laboratory, and a peace process that never quite ends.

legalRegimes.name: Inner Line
legalRegimes.note: Colonial inner line still structures who may enter.

name: Mizo insurgency
summary: Mizo National Front uprising from 1966, including the air action on Aizawl, through two decades of guerrilla war to the 1986 peace accord and Mizoram statehood.
scaleRationale: A full insurgency that actually ended in a durable accord.

accords.name: Mizo Accord
accords.outcome: Mizoram state; MNF entered electoral politics

name: Naxal–Maoist conflict
summary: From the 1967 Naxalbari uprising through the 2004 CPI (Maoist) merger, a rural revolutionary insurgency across a ‘red corridor’ of central and eastern India.
scaleRationale: Multi-state, multi-decade, still active in pockets.

locations.name: Srikakulam
locations.note: Girijan uprising 1968–70; plains leadership broken at Sompeta, 1969.

locations.name: Jehanabad
locations.note: Central Bihar Maoist–Ranvir Sena belt; 2005 jailbreak.

locations.name: Gadchiroli
locations.note: Western Dandakaranya; C-60 operations and 2019 nallah blast.

peoples.name: Adivasi communities of Bastar, Jharkhand, Odisha

sources.title: Civilians biggest casualty of Naxal violence
sources.creator: The Hindu, citing MHA RTI
sources.note: MHA series from 1980: 20,012 dead by 30 March 2015 (12,146 civilians, 3,105 security forces, 4,761 LWE).

sources.title: Fatalities in Left-wing Extremism, 1999–2018 (MHA)
sources.creator: SATP compilation of Ministry of Home Affairs
sources.note: MHA 1999–15 May 2018: 7,869 civilians, 2,691 SF, 3,274 Naxalite, total 13,834.

killed.note: MHA LWE tables typically start around 1980 and split civilians, security forces and LWE. SATP news counts diverge on who is a civilian. Srikakulam 1968–70 and Calcutta 1970–72 sit partly outside the MHA LWE series. 2015 already stood at about 20,000; later operations and pre-1980 killings push a full-campaign band into the low-to-mid 20,000s.

sources.title: MHA annual reports on Left Wing Extremism
sources.creator: Ministry of Home Affairs

name: Assam Movement
summary: Mass agitation (1979–1985) against ‘foreigners’ in Assam, mixing student politics, ethnic fear, and a demand to recast the electoral roll. The 1985 Assam Accord did not close the question.
scaleRationale: Six years, statewide, and Nellie inside it.

parties.note: Movement leadership; not a conventional militia.

accords.name: Assam Accord
accords.outcome: Citizenship cut-off date of 24 March 1971; NRC later

name: Nellie, 1983
summary: A few hours of mass killing in villages around Nellie, Assam, during the boycotted 1983 state election. Mostly Bengali-speaking Muslim peasants died. Almost no convictions.
scaleRationale: A single morning, but among the deadliest episodes in independent India.

peoples.name: Tiwa / Lalung and other local peasants

sources.title: Official count often given as 1,819; journalists and later writers go higher.
Makiko Kimura, The Nellie Massacre of 1983
sources.creator: Makiko Kimura

name: ULFA insurgency
summary: United Liberation Front of Asom, founded 1979, waged an armed independence campaign from Assam with alleged camps across the Bangladesh and Myanmar borders, then splintered through talks and operations.
scaleRationale: State-level insurgency with cross-border logistics, decades long.

name: Bodo insurgency
summary: Bodo armed groups (NDFB and others) fought for a homeland on the north bank of the Brahmaputra. Cycles of rebellion, accord, split, and communal targeting of Adivasi and Muslim settlers.
scaleRationale: Repeated campaigns plus civilian massacres; multiple accords.

name: Tripura insurgency
summary: Tribal insurgent groups (NLFT, ATTF) fought a state where partition-era and later migration had made the indigenous Tripuri a demographic minority. Violence fell after the 2000s.
scaleRationale: Years of killings and displacement in a small state.

name: Punjab / Khalistan insurgency
summary: Sikh militant campaign for Khalistan, the 1984 army assault on the Golden Temple, Indira Gandhi’s assassination, and the Delhi killings that followed.
scaleRationale: A state-level war plus a capital pogrom; still politically live.

name: Kashmir insurgency
summary: Armed insurgency in the Valley from 1989, with militant groups, heavy militarisation, displacement of Kashmiri Pandits, and alleged Pakistani support. The dispute sits on the 1947 war.
scaleRationale: Decades, high fatalities, internationalised.

sources.title: Šumit Ganguly, The Crisis in Kashmir
sources.creator: Sumit Ganguly

name: Bombay riots, 1992–93
summary: Weeks of communal killing in Bombay after the Babri Masjid demolition, followed by the March 1993 bombings. The Srikrishna Commission mapped both the riots and the politics around them.
scaleRationale: A megacity, hundreds to thousands dead, lasting urban geography.

name: Kargil War, 1999
summary: Limited war after Pakistani soldiers and militants occupied ridgelines on the Indian side of the LoC in the Kargil district. Nuclear-armed neighbours, high-altitude fighting, US diplomacy.
scaleRationale: A short interstate war, geographically tight, politically huge.

name: Gujarat, 2002
summary: After the Godhra train burning, weeks of anti-Muslim violence across Gujarat. Death tolls, state complicity, and the legal aftermath remain politically radioactive.
scaleRationale: Statewide pogrom with a documented death toll in the hundreds to thousands and national aftershocks.

peoples.name: Gujarati Muslims
peoples.role: primary victims of the post-Godhra killings

sources.title: Official Gujarat figures vs independent estimates (HRW, Concerned Citizens Tribunal)
Human Rights Watch, ‘We Have No Orders to Save You’
Concerned Citizens Tribunal, Crime Against Humanity

name: Mumbai attacks, 2008
summary: Coordinated shooting and bombing attacks in Mumbai by Lashkar-e-Taiba gunmen who arrived by sea. An external strike on a city, not a riot.
scaleRationale: Hours, one city, high symbolic charge; fatalities in the low hundreds.

sources.title: Indian investigation / UN 1267 listings of LeT

name: Manipur, 2023–
summary: Ethnic violence between Meitei and Kuki-Zo communities after a high-court order on Scheduled Tribe status. Thousands of weapons looted, hills and valley partitioned in practice, a still-moving death and displacement count.
scaleRationale: A small state, years of displacement, hundreds dead — not a riot that ended in a week.

name: Bombay serial blasts, 1993
summary: Thirteen coordinated bombs across Bombay on 12 March 1993. Courts tied the conspiracy to Dawood Ibrahim’s network, staged from abroad as revenge for the riots.
scaleRationale: One afternoon, a megacity, hundreds dead; a transnational crime-terror plot.

name: IC-814 hijack
summary: Indian Airlines flight 814 was hijacked to Kandahar in December 1999. India released three jailed militants, including Masood Azhar, who later founded Jaish-e-Mohammed.
scaleRationale: One aircraft, one week, a political ransom with a long afterlife.

locations.name: Kandahar (flight originated in Kathmandu, via Amritsar/Dubai)

sources.title: Indian Ministry of External Affairs / contemporary reporting, December 1999

name: Parliament attack, 2001
summary: Five gunmen entered the Parliament complex in New Delhi on 13 December 2001. India blamed Jaish-e-Mohammed and Lashkar-e-Taiba. The crisis ran to mobilisation on the border.
scaleRationale: A single morning at the capital’s core; the military sequel was large.

name: Delhi serial blasts, 2005
summary: Three bombs in Delhi markets on 29 October 2005, just before Diwali and Eid. Police named a Pakistan-based network. The dead were shoppers.
scaleRationale: One evening, a capital, dozens dead.

name: Mumbai train blasts, 2006
summary: Seven bombs on Western Railway suburban trains in Mumbai at rush hour on 11 July 2006. Investigators named Lashkar-e-Taiba and local modules.
scaleRationale: A city’s commuting spine, more than 180 dead in one evening.

name: Pathankot airbase, 2016
summary: Gunmen attacked the IAF base at Pathankot in January 2016. India named Jaish-e-Mohammed. The fight lasted days inside a military station.
scaleRationale: A military base, not a city market; still an external strike on Indian soil.

name: Uri, 2016
summary: A fidayeen attack on an army camp at Uri in September 2016 killed eighteen soldiers. India named Jaish-e-Mohammed and answered with announced strikes across the Line of Control.
scaleRationale: One camp, a morning, then a diplomatic-military crisis.

name: Pulwama, 2019
summary: A Jaish-e-Mohammed suicide bomber drove into a CRPF convoy on the Jammu–Srinagar highway on 14 February 2019. Forty troopers were killed. Balakot followed.
scaleRationale: The deadliest attack on Indian security forces in Kashmir in years, with an interstate sequel.

sources.title: Government of India / The Hindu, February 2019

name: Akshardham temple attack, 2002
summary: Two gunmen entered the Swaminarayan Akshardham complex in Gandhinagar on 24 September 2002. NSG ended the siege at dawn. India named Lashkar-e-Taiba and Jaish-e-Mohammed; the Supreme Court later acquitted six Indians of a local conspiracy.
scaleRationale: One night at a temple, tens dead; an external raid, not a riot.

name: Hyderabad twin blasts, 2007
summary: Two bombs at Lumbini Park and Gokul Chat in Koti on 25 August 2007. An NIA court later convicted Indian Mujahideen operatives; Riyaz Bhatkal was named as a planter still abroad.
scaleRationale: One Saturday evening, two sites, tens dead.

sources.title: The Indian Express / The Hindu, Hyderabad 2007

name: Indian Mujahideen urban bombings, 2008–13
summary: A SIMI splinter calling itself Indian Mujahideen emailed claims before bicycle and tiffin bombs in Jaipur, Ahmedabad and Delhi in 2008, then Mumbai in 2011 and Dilsukhnagar in 2013. Investigators described an Indian module with alleged Lashkar links.
scaleRationale: Several cities over five years, hundreds dead; a named urban campaign.

sources.title: The Hindu / Reuters / Indian Express, IM 2008–13

name: Pune German Bakery blast, 2010
summary: A bomb in an unattended bag at the German Bakery in Koregaon Park. Seventeen people were killed, including foreigners. Maharashtra ATS charged a Lashkar module working with Indian Mujahideen operatives.
scaleRationale: One café, one evening.

name: Gurdaspur / Dinanagar attack, 2015
summary: Three gunmen in army fatigues crossed into Punjab, fired on a bus and stormed the Dinanagar police station. Intelligence Bureau officials described a Lashkar-e-Taiba method; GPS sets pointed back across the border.
scaleRationale: One town, one day, a fidayeen raid out of Kashmir into the plains.
